newsitem.title: UK: Airlines say sidestepped Iraq oil price jump.
newsitem.headline: Airlines say sidestepped Iraq oil price jump.

text.p: Airlines said on Thursday they have sidestepped the oil price leap sparked by the Iraq crisis and have not been stung as some were during the Gulf War period.
But oil traders doubted they have been nimble enough to avoid fully the impact of a market that had risen steadily even before the U.S. launched its missiles on Iraq.

After the 1990 invasion of Kuwait jet fuel prices soared above $500 a tonne, but since then airlines say they have become shrewder and now claim to hedge most of their purchases by buying fuel in advance.
"We have a risk mangement plan in place which is designed to cope with this kind of eventuality," said a spokeswoman for British Airways Plc one of the world's largest carriers.
Airlines buy oil in advance on the futures and derivatives markets. When they eventually need the real oil they simply exchange futures for physical cargoes of jet fuel.

But despite their claims, oil traders think some airlines got it wrong this year by failing to buy during the summer when, for a few weeks, prices languished below $200 a tonne. "They didn't want to buy in the spring because prices were too high and then they held off again hoping the oil-for-food deal with Iraq would push prices lower," said a trader at a Wall Street bank who specialises in jet fuel.
Jet prices jumped about five percent this week to near $245 after the oil-for-food deal between Iraq and the United Nations was put on ice. Crude jumped more than $1 a barrel on the news.

The latest price rise pile pressure on airlines who have not hedged. This year's prices are averaging some 25 percent above 1995 levels. Compounding the risk, European airlines are exposed to exchange rates as well as oil price jumps when buying fuel.

The dollar, the currency of the international oil trade, has gained against the mark and most other European currencies over the past year. The average mark rate in 1996 is running more than four percent over the whole 1995 average.
"We have been hit by the dollar and jet prices over the last year," said a jet buyer at a European airline.

"We estimate our jet costs will rise 20 to 30 percent this year compared to last," he added but expected only modest costs to be passed on to the consumer. "Competition is severe so airlines don't want to raise prices in case they lose market share. But I do think results will be hit," he said.
Oil traders say the market for jet fuel was fundamentally strong even before the Iraqi oil deal was delayed.

Asian demand has been very strong in recent weeks they say and the market looked set for big gains in the fourth quarter. Stocks of middle distillates, from which jet fuel is drawn, are low in the West and in Europe tough new green rules for diesel fuel threaten to keep the market tight.
Holiday firms are also trying to keep their customers protected and see little chance of price hikes in holidays.

"A 10 percent rise in jet fuel prices usually means a one cent rise in costs to the tour operator," said Keith Betton, head of corporate affairs at the Britain's Association of British Travel Agent (ABTA).
For a short-haul holiday costing 300 stg about 100 stg goes to the airline and of that about 30 stg is for fuel, he said. ABTA represents 620 U.K. tour operators and 7000 travel agents.
A five percent price rise means just 1.50 stg extra -- well below the amount most travel companies would pass on.
"Administration costs are more than the price hike itself so most won't bother," said an industry source.
